newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Criticised EU meets over Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Criticised EU meets over Zaire.

text.p: European Union aid ministers, stung by French criticism of "spineless inaction" in the plight of refugees stranded in eastern Zaire, met on Thursday to seek a joint response to the deepening human crisis.
Arriving for the meeting in Brussels, Humanitarian Aid Commissioner Emma Bonino said something had to be done urgently to help the estimated 1.2 million refugees from Rwanda and Burundi.
"My feeling is that it is not time any longer for political reports, a strong call has to come from this meeting," Bonino told Reuters.

She wants the international community to open safe corridors into the region to facilitate food deliveries and the return of refugees caught by the fighting between Tutsi rebels and the Zairean army in the region.
Diplomats said she would also push for some form of military protection for the corridors, an issue which has paralysed a world reluctant to become involved in another African crisis.

The EU has offered to help create and finance an African force, but seven regional leaders meeting in Nairobi on Tuesday said they wanted the United Nations to create a "neutral force" to come to the rescue of the refugees.
France and Spain have offered troops but the rest of the world has remained silent.
Aldo Ajello, the EU's special envoy to the Great Lakes region, said the Nairobi conference had helped to crystallise the debate. "Now, we have to see which countries are ready to send troops."
The United States, with memories still fresh of its ill-fated intervention in Somalia four years ago, has indicated it would support a force but would not commit troops itself.

Shortly before the Brussels meeting started, France accused the international community of being spineless on Wednesday as it vented its frustration at the poor response to a proposed multinational force to help avert a refugee disaster in Zaire.

"I'm knocking on doors, asking if anyone is prepared to assume his responsibilities. The answer is 'Could you come back tomorrow', or 'We might lend an aircraft'," Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told LCI television.
"The main obstacle is the international community's spinelessness," he said.

Meanwhile, a Zairean envoy in South Africa said on Thursday that President Nelson Mandela had promised to play a big role in peace efforts in the region, but it was not immediately clear what his role would be.

"(Zairean) President Mobutu has asked his colleague (Mandela) to play a major diplomatic role in this conflict...and he is going to play the role that is expected from him in the situation that is occurring in Zaire," Zairean special envoy Honore Ngbanda, told a news conference on Thursday, a day after he held talks with Mandela.
The U.S. would like South Africa, economically and political Africa's giant, to take more responsibility for the continent's woes, but Mandela is cautious of becoming drawn into never-ending crises.
